subject: math
title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
seo_title: Grade 4 Comparing and Ordering Fractions Worksheets (BC Curriculum) – Free with Answer Key
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on comparing and ordering fractions for the BC curriculum: name fractions, equivalent fractions, same denominator or numerator, benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key. Good FSA practice.
key_big: Same bottom number: compare the top numbers. Same top number: more parts means smaller parts.
key_sub: 3/8 < 5/8, and 1/8 < 1/4. Use 0, 1/2 and 1 as benchmarks, and only compare fractions of the same whole.
body_html:
The idea

A fraction names equal parts of a whole. The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole has. The top number (numerator) tells how many parts you count.

The whole can be a shape or a set. If 2 of 6 counters are green, then 26 of the set is green.

Equivalent fractions

Different fractions can show the same amount. Cut every part into 2 and you get twice as many parts, and twice as many are shaded.

Same denominator: compare the top numbers

When the bottom numbers are the same, the pieces are the same size. More pieces means more.

Same numerator: more parts means smaller parts

When the top numbers are the same, you have the same number of pieces. Then look at the size of the pieces. A whole cut into more parts has smaller parts.

Example

Compare 34 and 38.

Both have 3 pieces. Fourths are bigger than eighths.

Answer: 34 > 38

Benchmarks: 0, 12 and 1

Ask: is the fraction close to 0, close to 12 or close to 1? To check 12, compare the top number with half of the bottom number.

Example

Order 56, 18 and 38 from least to greatest.

18 and 38 are both eighths, and 1 < 3. Both are less than 12. 56 is more than 12.

Answer: 18, 38, 56

WhenTryExample
Same bottom numberCompare the top numbers38 < 58
Same top numberFewer parts means bigger parts23 > 25
One is below 12, one is aboveBenchmark 1225 < 710
One is more than 1, one is lessBenchmark 154 > 78

Use the same whole

Compare fractions only when they are parts of the same size whole. Half of a large pizza can be more than 34 of a small pizza.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking 18 > 14 because 8 > 4A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces
Counting only the white parts for the bottom number: calling 3 of 5 shaded 32The bottom number counts all the equal parts: 35
Naming parts that are not equalA fraction needs equal parts
Adding to make equivalent fractions: 12 = 34Multiply the top and bottom by the same number: 12 = 24
Comparing parts of different-size wholesMake sure both fractions are of the same whole

faq.q: What fractions do Grade 4 students learn in BC?
faq.a: In the BC curriculum, Grade 4 students compare and order fractions, use models to see equal fractions such as 1/2 = 2/4, and use benchmarks such as 0, 1/2 and 1. They also connect tenths and hundredths to decimals.
Both are one piece of the same whole. A whole cut into 8 equal parts has smaller parts than a whole cut into 4, so 1/8 < 1/4.
A benchmark is an easy number to compare with, like 0, 1/2 or 1. For example, 3/8 is less than 1/2 and 5/6 is close to 1, so 3/8 < 5/6.

faq.q: Do fractions help with the Grade 4 FSA?
faq.a: The Grade 4 FSA numeracy section checks how students reason with numbers. Comparing fractions with pictures and benchmarks builds that number sense.

sets.title: Name fractions of shapes and sets

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: There are 3 equal parts and 1 is shaded. So 13 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: There are 5 equal parts and 3 are shaded. So 35 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: There are 8 equal parts and 5 are shaded. So 58 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: There are 6 equal parts and 4 are shaded. So 46 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.e: There are 4 equal parts and 3 are shaded. So 34 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.e: There are 10 equal parts and 7 are shaded. So 710 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: There are 8 equal parts and 3 are shaded. So 38 is shaded. The bottom number counts all the equal parts, not just the white ones.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is not shaded?
items.e: There are 5 equal parts. 2 are shaded, so 5 − 2 = 3 are not shaded. The answer is 35. The bottom number counts all the equal parts.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is not shaded?
items.e: There are 6 equal parts. 1 is shaded, so 6 − 1 = 5 are not shaded. The answer is 56. The bottom number counts all the equal parts.

items.q: What fraction of the counters are green?
items.e: The whole is the set of 6 counters. 2 of them are green, so 26 of the set is green. Do not compare green with white (2 to 4).

items.q: What fraction of the counters are green?
items.e: The whole is the set of 8 counters. 3 of them are green, so 38 of the set is green. Do not compare green with white (3 to 5).

items.q: What fraction of the counters are green?
items.e: The whole is the set of 10 counters. 4 of them are green, so 410 of the set is green. Do not compare green with white (4 to 6).

items.q: What fraction of the counters are not green?
items.e: There are 9 counters in the set. 2 are green, so 9 − 2 = 7 are not green. The answer is 79.

items.q: A bag has 4 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. What fraction of the marbles are blue?
items.e: The whole set is 4 + 3 = 7 marbles. 3 are blue, so 37 are blue. 34 compares blue with red; it does not use the whole set.

items.q: A box has 12 pencil crayons. 5 of them are broken. What fraction of the pencil crayons are broken?
items.e: There are 12 pencil crayons in the whole set and 5 are broken. So 512 are broken.

items.q: Which picture shows 34 shaded?
items.e: Picture C has 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. Picture A has 4 parts, but they are not equal. B shows 14 and D shows 35.

items.q: Which picture shows 23 shaded?
items.e: Picture D has 3 equal parts with 2 shaded. Picture B has 3 parts, but they are not equal. A shows 13 and C shows 25.

items.q: Leah says 14 of this bar is shaded. Is she right?
c: No. It shows 34.
No. It shows 13.
No. The 4 parts are not equal.
items.e: No. The 4 parts are not equal. A fraction names equal parts of a whole. The shaded part is bigger than the other parts, so it is more than 14.

items.q: These 4 counters are 13 of a set. How many counters are in the whole set?
items.e: 13 means the set has 3 equal groups, and this is 1 group. 3 groups of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12 counters.

items.q: These 5 counters are 12 of a set. How many counters are in the whole set?
items.e: 12 means the set has 2 equal groups, and this is 1 group. 2 groups of 5 is 2 × 5 = 10 counters.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
12 = ?4
items.e: The bottom bar has 4 equal parts, so each half of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 1 half becomes 1 × 2 = 2 fourths. So 12 = 24.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
13 = ?6
items.e: The bottom bar has 6 equal parts, so each third of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 1 third becomes 1 × 2 = 2 sixths. So 13 = 26.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
12 = ?8
items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each half of the top bar is cut into 4 parts. 1 half becomes 1 × 4 = 4 eighths. So 12 = 48.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
24 = ?8
items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each fourth of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 2 fourths become 2 × 2 = 4 eighths. So 24 = 48.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
23 = ?6
items.e: The bottom bar has 6 equal parts, so each third of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 2 thirds become 2 × 2 = 4 sixths. So 23 = 46.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
34 = ?8
items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each fourth of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 3 fourths become 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.q:
The bars are the same size, and the shaded parts are equal.
25 = ?10
items.e: The bottom bar has 10 equal parts, so each fifth of the top bar is cut into 2 parts. 2 fifths become 2 × 2 = 4 tenths. So 25 = 410.

items.q:
Look at the three bars. Which number is missing?
12 = 24 = ?8
items.e: All three bars are shaded to the same place. The bottom bar has 8 parts and 4 are shaded, so 12 = 24 = 48. The numbers double each time: 1, 2, 4 and 2, 4, 8.

items.q:
The circle has 8 equal parts. 68 is shaded.
68 = ?4
items.e: Put the 8 parts in groups of 2. That makes 4 equal groups. The 6 shaded parts make 6 ÷ 2 = 3 groups. So 68 = 34.

items.q:
The circle has 6 equal parts. 46 is shaded.
46 = ?3
items.e: Put the 6 parts in groups of 2. That makes 3 equal groups. The 4 shaded parts make 4 ÷ 2 = 2 groups. So 46 = 23.

items.q:
The circle has 10 equal parts. 810 is shaded.
810 = ?5
items.e: Put the 10 parts in groups of 2. That makes 5 equal groups. The 8 shaded parts make 8 ÷ 2 = 4 groups. So 810 = 45.

items.q:
The circle has 8 equal parts. 28 is shaded.
28 = ?4
items.e: Put the 8 parts in groups of 2. That makes 4 equal groups. The 2 shaded parts make 2 ÷ 2 = 1 group. So 28 = 14.

items.q:
The arrow points to 12. Use the bottom number line.
12 = ?8
items.e: Follow the dashed line down. It lands on mark 4 of 8 on the bottom line, so 12 = 48.

items.q:
The arrow points to 25. Use the bottom number line.
25 = ?10
items.e: Follow the dashed line down. It lands on mark 4 of 10 on the bottom line, so 25 = 410.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 12?
items.e: Half of 8 is 4, so 48 = 12. 38 is less than half and 58 is more than half. 14 has the same top number, but fourths are smaller than halves.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 23?
items.e: Cut each third into 2 equal parts: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6, so 23 = 46. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.

items.q: Which fraction is not equal to 12?
items.e: Half of 4 is 2, half of 10 is 5 and half of 6 is 3, so 24, 510 and 36 are all equal to 12. Half of 8 is 4, not 3, so 38 is not equal to 12.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Compare the shaded parts.
items.e: Both bars are shaded to the same place. The bottom bar has more parts, but each part is smaller. So they are equal: 12 = 24.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Compare the shaded parts.
items.e: 34 is the same as 68, and the bottom bar has 58 shaded. So the top bar has more: 34 > 58. More shaded parts does not always mean more shaded.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Compare the shaded parts.
items.e: 13 is the same as 26, and the bottom bar has 36 shaded. So the bottom bar has more: 13 < 36. More shaded parts does not always mean more shaded.

sets.title: Compare with the same denominator or numerator

items.q: The two bars are the same size. Which statement is true?
c: 35 > 25
35 < 25
35 = 25
25 > 35
items.e: Both are fifths, so the pieces are the same size. 3 fifths is more than 2 fifths, so 35 > 25.

items.q: The two bars are the same size. Which statement is true?
c: 78 < 48
48 = 78
48 < 78
48 > 78
items.e: Both are eighths, so the pieces are the same size. 4 eighths is less than 7 eighths, so 48 < 78.

items.q: Compare 56 and 16. Which statement is true?
c: 56 > 16
56 < 16
56 = 16
16 > 56
items.e: Both are sixths, so the pieces are the same size. 5 sixths is more than 1 sixth, so 56 > 16.

items.q: Compare 710 and 910. Which statement is true?
c: 710 > 910
710 < 910
710 = 910
910 < 710
items.e: Both are tenths, so the pieces are the same size. 7 tenths is less than 9 tenths, so 710 < 910.

items.q: Compare 23 and 13. Which statement is true?
c: 23 = 13
23 < 13
13 > 23
23 > 13
items.e: Both are thirds, so the pieces are the same size. 2 thirds is more than 1 third, so 23 > 13.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: All four are eighths, so the pieces are the same size. 7 is the most pieces, so 78 is the greatest.

items.q:
Order from least to greatest:
410, 910, 110
c: 410, 910, 110
410, 110, 910
910, 410, 110
110, 410, 910
items.e: All are tenths, so compare the top numbers: 1 < 4 < 9. So the order is 110, 410, 910.

items.q: 24 of bar A is shaded. 34 of bar B is shaded. Ethan says the picture shows 24 > 34. What is wrong?
c: Nothing. 24 > 34.
He should count the white parts.
Both bars have 4 parts, so they are equal.
items.e: The bars are different wholes. Bar A is longer than bar B, so 24 of A can look as big as 34 of B. Compare fractions of the same whole: 24 < 34.

items.q: The two bars are the same size. Which statement is true?
c: 14 < 18
14 > 18
18 > 14
14 = 18
items.e: Both have 1 piece. Fourths are bigger than eighths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 14 > 18.

items.q: The two circles are the same size. Which statement is true?
c: 13 < 16
16 < 13
16 > 13
16 = 13
items.e: Both have 1 piece. Thirds are bigger than sixths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 16 < 13.

items.q: Compare 110 and 15. Which statement is true?
c: 15 < 110
110 = 15
110 > 15
110 < 15
items.e: Both have 1 piece. Fifths are bigger than tenths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 110 < 15. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.

items.q: Compare 16 and 112. Which statement is true?
c: 16 < 112
16 = 112
16 > 112
112 > 16
items.e: Both have 1 piece. Sixths are bigger than twelfths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 16 > 112. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.

items.q: Compare 1100 and 110. Which statement is true?
c: 1100 < 110
1100 = 110
110 < 1100
1100 > 110
items.e: Both have 1 piece. Tenths are bigger than hundredths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 1100 < 110. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.

items.q: Compare 34 and 38. Which statement is true?
c: 38 > 34
34 > 38
34 = 38
34 < 38
items.e: Both have 3 pieces. Fourths are bigger than eighths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 34 > 38.

items.q: Compare 25 and 23. Which statement is true?
c: 25 = 23
25 > 23
25 < 23
23 < 25
items.e: Both have 2 pieces. Thirds are bigger than fifths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 25 < 23.

items.q: Compare 56 and 510. Which statement is true?
c: 56 > 510
510 > 56
56 < 510
56 = 510
items.e: Both have 5 pieces. Sixths are bigger than tenths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 56 > 510.

items.q: Which fraction is the smallest?
items.e: All four are 1 piece. The biggest bottom number makes the smallest pieces, so 110 is the smallest.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: All four have 3 pieces. The smallest bottom number makes the biggest pieces, so 34 is the greatest.

items.q:
Order from least to greatest:
13, 18, 15
c: 18, 13, 15
13, 18, 15
18, 15, 13
13, 15, 18
items.e: All are 1 piece. More parts means smaller parts: eighths are the smallest and thirds are the biggest. So the order is 18, 15, 13.

items.q: Liam says 18 > 14 because 8 > 4. Is he right?
c: No. 18 = 14.
No. Eighths are smaller than fourths.
items.e: No. Eighths are smaller than fourths. Cut the same whole into 8 parts and each part is smaller than when you cut it into 4 parts. So 18 < 14.

sets.title: Order fractions and use benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1

items.q: The dot shows 18. Which benchmark is 18 closest to: 0, 12 or 1?
items.e: 18 is closest to 0: it is only 18 away from 0.

items.q: The dot shows 910. Which benchmark is 910 closest to: 0, 12 or 1?
items.e: 910 is closest to 1: it is only 110 away from 1.

items.q: Which benchmark is 25 closest to: 0, 12 or 1?
items.e: 25 is closest to 12: it is only 110 away from 12.

items.q: Which benchmark is 56 closest to: 0, 12 or 1?
items.e: 56 is closest to 1: it is only 16 away from 1.

items.q: Where is 38?
items.e: Half of 8 is 4. 3 is less than 4, so 38 is less than 12. So the answer is less than 12.

items.q: Where is 510?
items.e: Half of 10 is 5, so 510 is exactly 12. So the answer is exactly 12.

items.q: Where is 46?
items.e: Half of 6 is 3. 4 is more than 3, so 46 is more than 12. So the answer is between 12 and 1. It is less than 1 because 4 is less than 6.

items.q: Where is 54?
items.e: The top number (5) is bigger than the bottom number (4), so 54 is greater than 1: 44 = 1 whole and 14 more.

items.q: Compare 38 and 46. Which statement is true?
c: 46 < 38
38 > 46
38 = 46
38 < 46
items.e: Use 12 as a benchmark. Half of 8 is 4. 3 is less than 4, so 38 is less than 12. Half of 6 is 3. 4 is more than 3, so 46 is more than 12. So 38 < 46.

items.q: Compare 25 and 712. Which statement is true?
c: 25 > 712
25 = 712
712 < 25
25 < 712
items.e: Use 12 as a benchmark. Double the top: 2 × 2 = 4, which is less than 5, so 25 is less than 12. Half of 12 is 6. 7 is more than 6, so 712 is more than 12. So 25 < 712.

items.q: Compare 56 and 410. Which statement is true?
c: 410 > 56
56 > 410
56 < 410
56 = 410
items.e: Use 12 as a benchmark. Half of 6 is 3. 5 is more than 3, so 56 is more than 12. Half of 10 is 5. 4 is less than 5, so 410 is less than 12. So 56 > 410.

items.q: Compare 54 and 78. Which statement is true?
c: 54 < 78
78 > 54
54 = 78
54 > 78
items.e: Use 1 as a benchmark. 54 is more than 1 (the top is bigger than the bottom). 78 is less than 1 (the top is smaller than the bottom). So 54 > 78.

items.q: Which fraction is less than 12?
items.e: 46, 58 and 710 are all more than 12. Half of 12 is 6. 5 is less than 6, so 512 is less than 12. So 512 is the one less than 12.

items.q: Which fraction is greater than 12?
items.e: Double the top: 2 × 3 = 6, which is more than 5, so 35 is more than 12. Half of 10 is 5. 4 is less than 5, so 410 is less than 12. Half of 12 is 6, so 612 is exactly 12. Half of 8 is 4. 2 is less than 4, so 28 is less than 12. A small top number like 3 can still be more than half.

items.q:
Order from least to greatest:
78, 15, 12
c: 15, 12, 78
12, 15, 78
78, 12, 15
78, 15, 12
items.e: 15 is less than 12 and 78 is more than 12. So the order is 15, 12, 78.

items.q:
Order from greatest to least:
13, 56, 12
c: 56, 12, 13
13, 56, 12
56, 13, 12
13, 12, 56
items.e: 56 is close to 1, and 13 is less than 12. So the order is 56, 12, 13.

items.q:
Order from greatest to least:
610, 310, 910
c: 610, 910, 310
310, 610, 910
910, 610, 310
610, 310, 910
items.e: All are tenths, so compare the top numbers: 9 > 6 > 3. So the order is 910, 610, 310.

items.q:
Order from least to greatest:
34, 110, 48
c: 34, 48, 110
110, 48, 34
110, 34, 48
34, 110, 48
items.e: 110 is close to 0. 48 is exactly 12. 34 is more than 12. So the order is 110, 48, 34.

items.q: Which letter shows 34?
items.e: 34 = 68. Count 6 eighths from 0: letter C is at 68. Letter A is at 28, which is a common mix-up.

items.q: Which letter shows 13?
items.e: 13 = 26. Count 2 sixths from 0: letter B is at 26. Letter C is at 36 = 12.

items.q: Ethan ate 38 of a pizza. Chloe ate 58 of the same pizza. Who ate more?
items.e: Both are eighths, so the pieces are the same size. 3 eighths is less than 5 eighths, so 38 < 58. So Chloe ate more.

items.q: Mateo hiked 34 of a trail in Stanley Park. Sofia hiked 35 of the same trail. Who hiked farther?
items.e: Both have 3 pieces. Fourths are bigger than fifths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 34 > 35. So Mateo hiked farther.

items.q: Emma’s family cut a pizza into 8 equal slices. Owen’s family cut the same size pizza into 4 equal slices. Emma and Owen each ate 1 slice. Who ate more pizza?
items.e: Emma ate 18 and Owen ate 14. The same pizza cut into fewer slices makes bigger slices, so 18 < 14. So Owen ate more.

items.q: At the Terry Fox Run, Zara walked 24 of the route. Ryan walked 12 of the same route. Who walked farther?
items.e: Half of 4 is 2, so 24 = 12. So they walked the same distance.

items.q: Liam biked 25 of the Stanley Park Seawall. Nadia biked 710 of the Seawall. Who biked farther?
items.e: Use 12 as a benchmark. Double the top: 2 × 2 = 4, which is less than 5, so 25 is less than 12. Half of 10 is 5. 7 is more than 5, so 710 is more than 12. So Nadia biked farther.

items.q: Arjun painted 46 of a fence. Jasleen painted 48 of the same fence. Who painted more?
items.e: Both have 4 pieces. Sixths are bigger than eighths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 46 > 48. So Arjun painted more.

items.q: On Grouse Mountain, Hana skied 13 of a ski run before she stopped. Lucas skied 12 of the same run before he stopped. Who skied farther before stopping?
items.e: Both are 1 piece. Halves are bigger than thirds, so 13 < 12. So Lucas skied farther.

items.q: Mei planted beans in 34 of a garden bed. Wei planted beans in 68 of a garden bed that is the same size. Who planted more of the bed?
items.e: Cut each fourth into 2 equal parts: 34 = 68. So they planted the same amount.

items.q: Owen and Nadia take BC Ferries from Vancouver to Victoria on the same route. Owen’s ferry has gone 58 of the way. Nadia’s ferry has gone 34 of the way. Whose ferry has gone farther?
c: They have gone the same distance
items.e: Write both in eighths: 34 = 68, and 5 < 6, so 58 < 34. So Nadia’s ferry has gone farther.

items.q: Simran ate 12 of a small pizza. Harjot ate 13 of a large pizza. Simran says she ate more because 12 > 13. Is she right?
c: Yes, because 12 > 13.
Not for sure. The pizzas are different sizes.
No, because 13 > 12.
items.e: The pizzas are different wholes. 13 of a large pizza can be more than 12 of a small pizza. Comparing 12 and 13 only works when the wholes are the same size. So: not for sure.

items.q: Olivia hiked 34 of a short trail near Kelowna. Noah hiked 12 of a long trail near Kamloops. Who hiked farther?
items.e: The trails are different wholes. 34 is more than 12 of the same trail, but the long trail may be many kilometres longer. Without the lengths, you can’t tell.

items.q: Jasleen ate 23 of her sandwich. Harjot ate 23 of his sandwich. Harjot’s sandwich is twice as long as Jasleen’s. Who ate more?
items.e: Both ate 23, but the wholes are different. 23 of a longer sandwich is more food, so Harjot ate more.

items.q: Four friends hiked the same trail on Vancouver Island. Kai hiked 12 of it, Leah hiked 38, Ryan hiked 78 and Ava hiked 14. Who hiked the farthest?
items.e: Use eighths: 12 = 48, 38, 78, 14 = 28. 7 eighths is the most, so Ryan hiked the farthest.

items.q: After a class party, four pizzas of the same size have some left. Pepperoni has 23 left, cheese has 16 left, veggie has 12 left and Hawaiian has 56 left. Which pizza has the least left?
items.e: Use sixths: 23 = 46, 16, 12 = 36, 56. 1 sixth is the least, so Cheese has the least left.

items.q: Kai, Leah and Owen are reading the same book. Kai has read 56 of it, Leah has read 16 and Owen has read 12. Order them from who has read the least to who has read the most.
items.e: Use sixths: 12 = 36. 1 < 3 < 5, so the order is Leah, Owen, Kai.

items.q: Ryan says 110 of a cake is more than 15 of the same cake because 10 > 5. Is he right?
c: No. They are the same size.
No. Tenths are smaller pieces than fifths.
items.e: No. Tenths are smaller pieces than fifths. The same cake cut into 10 pieces has smaller pieces than when it is cut into 5. So 110 < 15.

items.q: Ava’s class hiked 410 of a trail in Whistler before lunch. Did they hike more than half of the trail before lunch?
items.e: Half of 10 is 5. 4 is less than 5, so 410 is less than 12. So no, less than half.

items.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. 3 slices have mushrooms. What fraction of the pizza has mushrooms?
items.e: There are 8 equal slices in the whole pizza and 3 have mushrooms, so 38 has mushrooms. 58 has no mushrooms.

items.q: There are 6 canoes at a dock on the Fraser River. 3 of them are red. What fraction of the canoes are red?
items.e: The whole set is 6 canoes and 3 are red, so 36 of the canoes are red. (That is the same as 12.)

items.q: A trail has a sign at every 18 of the way. Sofia stops for a snack at the sign for 48. Which fraction is equal to 48?
items.e: Half of 8 is 4, so 48 = 12. Sofia is halfway along the trail.
